title: Bad deeds turned to good
hookLine: for those who repent and do good, Allah changes their bad deeds to good (25:70)
tomorrow: Block B close: prophets and light

lines: A LEDGER IS SUPPOSED TO BE PERMANENT.
THEN A LINE NO LEDGER ALLOWS.
cards: A ledger is supposed to be permanent. That's the whole point of one. Whatever goes in the red column stays there, and the best you can hope for is enough in the black to outweigh it.
Some people carry a version of that ledger around in their heads: a list of the worst things they've done.

The portrait of the servants of the Merciful has reached its hardest verses, the serious wrongs and what happens to someone who has done them. And the next line does something no ledger is supposed to do.

teach.b: Verses sixty-eight and sixty-nine name grave wrongs: calling on another god, killing a soul unjustly, adultery. Whoever does these, they say plainly, meets a heavy penalty.
Then verse seventy opens a door: except the one who repents, and believes, and does good work. "Allah will change their evil deeds to good deeds."
The verb is yubaddilu, to exchange, to swap one thing for another. Not erase. Exchange.
Commentators have read this in two ways. One is about this life. A person who turns around doesn't just stop the old habits; the energy that went into them starts going somewhere good.
The one who used to lie becomes careful with the truth. The one who used to take starts to give. The other reading goes further, and rests on a hadith in Muslim's collection.
On the Day of Judgment, a man is shown his small sins, one by one, while his great ones are held back. He braces himself. Then he's told: for each bad deed, you have a good one in its place.
And suddenly the man says, wait, I did other things too, I don't see them here. The Prophet ﷺ, telling this, laughed until his back teeth showed. Either way, the ledger isn't what it seemed.
The verse ends: God is ever Forgiving, Merciful. And the verse after says whoever repents and does good has truly turned to God.

how: Muslims describe repentance, tawba, as turning back to God with regret, stopping the wrong and resolving not to return to it; teachers often quote 25:70 to show that no one is beyond turning.

o: a record of deeds, which God can exchange for good
a scale that weighs deeds on the Day of Judgment
a list of sins that can never be changed or undone

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: 25:70 says repentance only erases bad deeds
the verb is exchange: God changes the bad deeds to good deeds.
scholars read the exchange both in this life and on the Day of Judgment
one reading is a changed life; another rests on a hadith in Muslim.
in the hadith, the man is relieved his great sins weren't shown
he asks where they are, hoping they'll be turned to good too.

games.q: on the Day of Judgment, you're shown your small sins one by one, and told each has been replaced with a good deed. your great sins haven't been shown. what do you say?
o: nothing, and hope no one notices.
wait, I did other things too. I don't see them here.
ask to see the full ledger first.
games.why: that's what the man in Muslim's hadith says, and the Prophet laughed until his back teeth showed.

practice: Think of one thing in your own red column, something you regret, and just name it without reliving it.
Then ask what its opposite would be, the good deed that could stand in its place: care, if you were careless; giving, if you took. If you pray, you can ask for it to be turned.

wordCard.voice: Ledger. The record this lesson overturns: for the one who repents, God exchanges the bad deeds for good ones. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: he exchanges, replaces; in 25:70 God exchanges bad deeds for good.

carryVoice: Your line: turned to good. The red column doesn't get the last word. Five hundred days, and that's a lot of mornings.

sources.q: Allah will change their evil deeds to good deeds.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 190 (the man whose sins are exchanged)
